messages.subject: Re: Same chi square for models with different responses
messages.subject_clean: Same chi square for models with different responses
messages.body_plain:
To be a little more specific, in both models the degree of freedom comes from asserting that the partial correlation of LDP and P is 0 conditional on Forest. So that is the same in both models. Yes, the outcome variable differs across models, but both models are saturated with respect to that variable--there are direct paths from every other variable to that variable in both models. So there is no chance for lack of fit elsewhere in the model to interact with lack of fit due to the specific constraint. So the fit statistics pretrty well have to be identical.

On Fri, Mar 31, 2017 at 7:19 PM, Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:
> The fit statistics for the two models are the same because the one restriction in the two models is the same. You have 1 DF in both cases because the one constraint on relations between variables--the one thing that stops both models from being saturated--is that there is no direct path or residual covariance between LDI and P. Both variables are dependent on Forest--that is the same across models So for both models the question is the same--does the joint dependency of LDI and P fully account for the covariance between LDI and P, or does it not, and if not, to what extent does it not?. In both cases, this joint dependency comes up short to the exact same extent, and so the fit statistics are identical.
>      Your parameter estimates are different, but the fit statistics in factor-based SEM are in no way a function of the parameter estimates--unlike regression, where you would expect different parameter estimates to be associated with, say, a different overall F statistic.

messages.subject: Re: Degrees of freedom with WLSMV as estimator and experimental data
messages.subject_clean: Degrees of freedom with WLSMV as estimator and experimental data
messages.body_plain:
> I investigated how the 4 exogenous variables affected the response Y1 and if Y2 has a mediating effect.

If Y1 and Y2 were both outcomes of the experiment, is it possible for Y2 to have affected Y1?

> Y2 has values from 1 to 7 and is set to ordered when running the model.

With this many ordered categories, it is probably better to treat Y2 as continuous.  If it is not approximately normal, you can use a robust estimator.

> when counting on my own (k(k+1)/2) I come to a different result. I already assume that the 6 thresholds for Y2 have to be taken into account, but I am not sure how.

There are 6 thresholds observed and estimated, so no df are gained from that part of the model.  The variance of the latent response underlying an ordinal variable is neither observed nor estimated, but its polyserial correlation with other variables is observed and estimated.  Again, no df gained because as you said, your model is saturated.  You can see the number of estimated parameters in the output of

fitMeasures(model.full, "npar")

> how the degrees of freedom are calculated when using ordinal endogenous variables and WLSMV as an estimator.

Still the number of observed summary statistics minus the number of estimated parameters.

> As I am dealing with experimental conditions I assume they are not correlated, but lavaan should account for that by default with fixed.x = TRUE.

fixed.x = TRUE means whatever their observed correlation is (including if it is zero, as expected in a balanced design), those values are assumed fixed rather than estimated.  So they are not included in the number of observed summary statistics or estimated parameters.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Latent Curve Model with Structured Residuals
messages.subject_clean: Latent Curve Model with Structured Residuals
messages.body_plain:
> Here is the model so far, and I'm wondering how to include the residual structure. Are "phantom variables," as seen in Curran's example input (attached), needed?:

Yes, you can do that like this:

e.rail1 =~ 1*rail1
rail1 ~~ 0*rail1
e.rail1 ~~ NA*e.rail1

e.rail2 =~ 1*rail2
rail2 ~~ 0*rail2
e.rail2 ~~ NA*e.rail2

e.rail2 ~ e.rail1
...

But I think it should not be necessary because lavaan will kind of make phantom latents automatically if you just include structural paths among residuals.  So they way you already have it should work.

rail2 ~ a1*rail1

Nothing wrong with trying it both ways, if you want to be sure and get some exercise experimenting with lavaan.

> out <- mplus2lavaan("M06.inp")
> summary(out$lav.out)
>
> Seems like it should be easy enough, but I receive this error:
>
> Read 80 items
> Error in parse(text = x, keep.source = FALSE) :
>   <text>:2:0: unexpected end of input
> 1: ~
>    ^

I'm not sure exactly what that error means, but I do not expect the direct translation from Mplus to lavaan to work in this instance.  In lavaan, you can only create new parameters that are functions of other parameters.  That is what Mplus is doing, but the "new(kappa)" utility is just not available in lavaan, as far as I know.  I think you can get the desired result by translating this part of Mplus syntax:

>  model constraint:           ! defining model constraint on alc predicting dep over time;
>   new(kappa);                       ! create "kappa" that corresponds to Eq 17 in paper;
>   deponalc3= deponalc2 + 1*kappa;   ! kappa serves to increment value of lagged effect;
>   deponalc4= deponalc2 + 2*kappa;   ! with each unit-passage of time;
>   deponalc5= deponalc2 + 3*kappa;

to look like this in lavaan, which just rearranges terms with some algebra, explicitly defines kappa, then constraints it:

kappa := deponalc3 - deponalc2
kappa == (deponalc4 - deponalc2) / 2
kappa == (deponalc5 - deponalc2) / 3

I think you used different parameter labels, so just update those.  I am unsure whether it is OK to constrain "kappa" twice, like I do above, but hopefully that works.  If not, you could create three kappas and constrain them to be equal.

kappa1 := deponalc3 - deponalc2
kappa2 := (deponalc4 - deponalc2) / 2
kappa3 := (deponalc5 - deponalc2) / 3
kappa1 == kappa2
kappa1 == kappa3

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: lavaan.mi: Error in checkSlotAssignment(object, name, value)
messages.subject_clean: lavaan.mi: Error in checkSlotAssignment(object, name, value)
messages.body_plain:
> Error in pd.solve(varcov, log.det = TRUE) : x appears to be not symmetric
> Any help deciphering this would be really appreciated.

I'm not sure where the problem is occurring, but apparently a matrix that is expected to be symmetric cannot be inverted by the pd.solve() function, which is in the mnormt package.  My guess is that a log-likelihood needs to be calculated for each observation, but the model-implied covariance matrix is NPD.  If you can send me a minimally reproducible example with data and syntax, then I can try to track down the error.  I may not be able to "fix" it if it just so happens to be the case that the pooled model-implied Sigma is NPD, but I can at least add a check for it and print a more informative error message.

If my suspicion above is correct, then you probably can't get even the chi-squared test (within indices) from anova(fit).  Is that what happens?  If so, you can avoid the likelihood-calculation issue altogether by using the D2 method for pooling chi-squared statistics:

anova(fit, test = "D2", indices = "all")

Unfortunately, D2 does not perform as well as D3 (inflated errors), but it is better than nothing.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

On Saturday, April 1, 2017 at 10:05:10 AM UTC-4, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > Here is the model so far, and I'm wondering how to include the residual structure. Are "phantom variables," as seen in Curran's example input (attached), needed?:
>
> Yes, you can do that like this:
>
> e.rail1 =~ 1*rail1
> rail1 ~~ 0*rail1
> e.rail1 ~~ NA*e.rail1
>
> e.rail2 =~ 1*rail2
> rail2 ~~ 0*rail2
> e.rail2 ~~ NA*e.rail2
>
> e.rail2 ~ e.rail1
> ...
>
> But I think it should not be necessary because lavaan will kind of make phantom latents automatically if you just include structural paths among residuals.  So they way you already have it should work.
>
> rail2 ~ a1*rail1
>
> Nothing wrong with trying it both ways, if you want to be sure and get some exercise experimenting with lavaan.
>
> > out <- mplus2lavaan("M06.inp")
> > summary(out$lav.out)
> >
> > Seems like it should be easy enough, but I receive this error:
> >
> > Read 80 items
> > Error in parse(text = x, keep.source = FALSE) :
> >   <text>:2:0: unexpected end of input
> > 1: ~
> >    ^
>
> I'm not sure exactly what that error means, but I do not expect the direct translation from Mplus to lavaan to work in this instance.  In lavaan, you can only create new parameters that are functions of other parameters.  That is what Mplus is doing, but the "new(kappa)" utility is just not available in lavaan, as far as I know.  I think you can get the desired result by translating this part of Mplus syntax:
>
> >  model constraint:           ! defining model constraint on alc predicting dep over time;
> >   new(kappa);                       ! create "kappa" that corresponds to Eq 17 in paper;
> >   deponalc3= deponalc2 + 1*kappa;   ! kappa serves to increment value of lagged effect;
> >   deponalc4= deponalc2 + 2*kappa;   ! with each unit-passage of time;
> >   deponalc5= deponalc2 + 3*kappa;
>
> to look like this in lavaan, which just rearranges terms with some algebra, explicitly defines kappa, then constraints it:
>
> kappa := deponalc3 - deponalc2
> kappa == (deponalc4 - deponalc2) / 2
> kappa == (deponalc5 - deponalc2) / 3
>
> I think you used different parameter labels, so just update those.  I am unsure whether it is OK to constrain "kappa" twice, like I do above, but hopefully that works.  If not, you could create three kappas and constrain them to be equal.
>
> kappa1 := deponalc3 - deponalc2
> kappa2 := (deponalc4 - deponalc2) / 2
> kappa3 := (deponalc5 - deponalc2) / 3
> kappa1 == kappa2
> kappa1 == kappa3
>

> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Dear all,

I am running a SEM model with 1 IV (OM_M), 3 DVs which covary (FC, EP, AC), 1 Mediator (RES) and several controls (LEEFTIJD, RULEOBEDIENCE, GESLACHT_D_VROUW)

I use the MLM Satorro Bentler

messages.body_plain:
I wanted just to signal that eliminating some multicollinearity in the starting variables (before imputation) has sorted out the issue. The ANOVA command works using the D3 test.
However, I there is a very bizarre issue, which I wanted to report. Perhaps it is me making a mistake somewhere. But hopefully, it could be useful for you to know.

With the imputed dataset I am using now, the configural factorial invariance model works with D3, the weak factorial invariance model [i.e., indicators constraints to be equal over time] works only with D2, and the strong factorial invariance model [intercepts of indicators constrained to be equal across time] works with D3. In other words, the issue with ANOVA now only arises with the weak factorial invariance model.

Best wishes,
Giovanni

messages.subject: Re: SEM & marker variable
messages.subject_clean: SEM & marker variable
messages.body_plain:
> I indeed find negative covariances between my latent variables

Negative covariances are not an indication of a nonpositive definite matrix.  Negative variances are (you have none of those) and out-of-bounds correlations are (i.e., > +/-1).  You can check for out-of-bounds correlations with lavInspect(fit, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>").  But you can have a NPD matrix even if neither of those particular "Heywood cases" are present.  If your variances and correlations are all within their natural boundaries, then your NPD matrix could have linear dependencies (redundancies, conceptually).

> I do not get why and how to fix this. Can anyone help me?

NPD matrices can be due to sampling error, or due to model misspecification.
To investigate whether misspecification is a plausible explanation, you can test the fit of your model(s).  To narrow down the source of misspecification, you can first fit a CFA.  Since the latent structure is saturated, all misfit is due to misspecification in the measurement model.  You may have to reconceptualize the measurement model before proceeding to test hypotheses about the latent constructs your hope are represented by your measurement model.  After establishing satisfactory fit in your CFA, then you can test the structural hypotheses by comparing the fit of the latent regression model to the CFA model.  Any decrement in fit will be due to imposing structural constraints.  This is sometimes called "the 2-step approach", and you can find more about it in the literature or by asking around on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>.
To investigate whether sampling error is a plausible explanation, you can check whether the 95% CI of an out-of-bounds estimate includes plausible values.  If you find a correlation > 1, you can transform the lower confidence limit of the covariance estimate into a correlation metric by dividing by its respective SDs.  http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0049124112442138

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
I don't think sending me private data is necessary, because we can narrow down what the problem is.  Either your pooled observed covariance matrices (i.e., the average S across imputations) or your pooled model-implied covariance matrix (i.e., Sigma calculated from pooled estimates) is NPD.  Unless you have out-of-bounds pooled parameter estimates, I'm guessing it is the pooled S that is NPD.
If I the pooled S is the NPD matrix, you should still be able to calculate the D3 chi-squared difference test between your configural and weak models, even if you can't get the overall D3 chi-squared for the weak model.  If that is the case, I would report the D3 test to compare models whenever possible, and just report D2 for a particular model if D3 is not available (and be transparent in your report -- e.g., make a table providing both D2 and D3 approaches for both individual-model tests and model-comparison tests).
Because you can get D3 for your configural model but not the weak model, I'm guessing that it is the Sigma estimate that is NPD (just for the weak model), which makes me think there must be an out-of-bounds pooled estimate that is the cause.  If so, then you will not be able to calculate the D3 chi-squared difference test between the configural and weak models, so use D2.
D2 has somewhat unpredictable Type I error rates, depending on the situation.  Another alternative would be to use the D1 statistic (a Wald test, see ?lavTestWald for a complete-data/FIML implementation), which has better Type I error control and only requires fitting the less constrained (e.g., configural) model for each test.  You calculate the D1 test statistic by specifying which (labeled) parameters should be constrained to equality, and this does not require fitting the weak model to test weak invariance.  (But you would have to fit the weak model to test strong invariance by testing the additional constraint of equal intercepts, but that would not require fitting the strong model.)  The caveat is you would have to identify the model using a marker variable (fixing a factor loading to 1 rather than the factor variance, and an intercept to zero instead of the factor mean), which assumes that the marker variable is in fact invariant.  If you reject the omnibus null hypothesis of weak invariance, then you would have to find out which parameters differ to establish partial invariance, and the chosen marker variable might actually not be invariant.  You could also do a sensitivity analysis by using different marker variables and seeing if your conclusions are consistent.

So the way forward is not straight-forward, but it is still possible to conduct valid tests if you plan them out carefully.

Good luck,

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

I am trying to run a model where my 4-level condition variable predicts interpersonal power, interpersonal power then predicts potential for success in the company, which in turn, predicts sense of belonging in the company.

model1 <- '

# outcome model

belong ~ c*condcc + b1*ipower + b2*potential

# mediator models

ipower ~ a1*condcc

potential ~ d1*ipower + a2*condcc

# indirect effects (IDE)

MEDSEQ1IDE  := a1*b1

MEDSEQ2IDE  := a2*b2

MEDSEQIDE  := a1*d1*b2

SumIDE  := (a1*d1*b2)

# total effect

total := c + (a1*b1) + (a2*b2) + (a1*d1*b2)

'

The model fit for that model was very poor and I was given the warning: "unordered factors(s) with more than 2 levels detected in data: condcc".

The next thing I tried was to created 3 new variables that reflected each of the contrast codes and entered those into the model together:

# outcome model

purePathBunkPowerIND := a3*b1

purPathBunkPotentialIND := a4*b2

bunkPathPotentialIND := a6*b2

bunkPathSEQIND := a5*d1*b2

SumIDE  := (a1*d1*b2) + (a3*d1*b2) + (a5*d1*b2)

# total effect

total := c1 + c2 + c3 +

         (a1*b1) + (a2*b2) +

         (a3*b1) + (a4*b2) +

         (a5*b1) + (a6*b2) +

         (a1*d1*b2) + (a3*d1*b2) + (a5*d1*b2)

'

But when I tried doing that but my model fit was still really messed up (RMSEA = 0.0000; SRMR = 0.0000, etc). I still get the same warning:  "unordered factors(s) with more than 2 levels detected in data: pureVpathbunk bunkVpath".

These error messages lead me to believe that I need to set these conditions as ordered. So I tried the following code where condition_f is the non-contrast coded variable

model3 <- '

# outcome model

belong ~ c*condition_f + b1*ipower + b2*potential

# mediator models

ipower ~ a1*condition_f

# indirect effects (IDE)

MEDSEQ1IDE  := a1*b1

MEDSEQ2IDE  := a2*b2

MEDSEQIDE  := a1*d1*b2

SumIDE  := (a1*d1*b2)

# total effect

total := c + (a1*b1) + (a2*b2) + (a1*d1*b2)

'

fit3 <- cfa(model3, data=dat,

            ordered = c("PURE","PATHWAY",

                        "BUNKER", "INCLUDE"))

But then I get the following error: lavaan WARNING: parameter table does not contain thresholds Error in lavsamplestats@cov[[g]][cbind(row.idx, col.idx)] :

  subscript out of bounds

I think the next step that I could do is to simply dummy code (as opposed to contrast coding) the 4-level condition variable but I do not want to do that because I am particularly interested in the differences between condition 2 and condition 3.

Alternatively,  maybe I can drop the condition variable and run the mediation analyses using group comparisons based on the condition variable? I think that would show me that the meditational model is different for each condition, and then I can look at the effect size of the indirect effect to see for which condition the indirect effect is the biggest?

Any help in this issue would be much appreciated!

messages.subject: Re: Question about chi^2 and fmin
messages.subject_clean: Question about chi^2 and fmin
messages.body_plain:
> But if the fmin value reported by lavaan is multiplied by 2, I got the same chi^2 and p-value as in the output.

Yes, that is correct.  The F_min reported in most SEM textbooks is calculated as

> log(det(Sigma)) - log(det(S)) + trace(S %*% solve(Sigma)) - p,

where p is the number of variables represented in S and Sigma.  However, that is valid only for complete data.  The F_min statistic is actually the average -2LL (negative 2 times the log-likelihood) across individuals in the sample, where each individual's -2LL compares the likelihood of that observation under the hypothesized (H0) model and unrestricted/saturated (H1) model.  That is why we multiply the F_min by N to get transform F_min (and average) into the -2LL for the full sample (a sum), because only the -2LL for the full sample is distributed as a chi-squared random variable under the standard assumptions (e.g., independent multivariate normal data, the H0 is true).

When you have missing data, the individual log-likelihoods for each observation under H0 and H1 are calculated using the submatrices of S and Sigma that correspond to which variables were observed for person i.  Those log-likelihoods are summed under each model, subtracted from each other, and multiplied by -2 to get the -2LL (likelihood ratio, chi-squared) test statistic.  Without any missing data, this method provides the same -2LL returned by F_min * N (i.e., the average -2LL times the sample size).

Regarding the "fmin" reported by lavaan, I think it is just in (negative) log-likelihood metric rather than (negative) 2-times-log-likelihood metric because minimizing F_min or (F_min / 2) leads to the same solution.  The log-likelihoods reported by fitMeasures() are also in log-likelihood metric rather than 2-times-log-likelihood metric, so I think it is just a convenience issue.  Notice that if you subtract the log-likelihoods and divide by N, you will get lavaan's "fmin" statistic:

example(cfa) # or example(sem)
fits <- fitMeasures(fit, c("logl","unrestricted.logl","ntotal","fmin","chisq"))
-(fits[["logl"]] - fits[["unrestricted.logl"]]) / fits[["ntotal"]]
fits[["fmin"]]

And multiplying the difference between log-likelihoods by -2 returns the chi-squared statistic.

-2*(fits[["logl"]] - fits[["unrestricted.logl"]])
fits[["chisq"]]

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: Complex path model indirect effct
messages.body_plain:
> I wanted to do calculate the direct and all indirect effects for a path analytic model... using the := symbol. But I am not sure how to use that in this slightly more complex model. How will that be coded?

The same way, using the := operator.  In the case of the 3-path indirect effect of V2 on V5 via V3 and V4, for example, you would define that indirect effect as the product of those 3 path coefficients.

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html

In more complex models, if you are unsure whether you have calculated all indirect effects, you can use matrix algebra after the model is fit.

fit <- sem(mySyntax, myData)
Beta <- lavInspect(fit, "est")$beta # matrix of path coefficients
# view effects of each order
Beta # direct effects
Beta %*% Beta # indirect effects involving 2 path coefficents
Beta %*% Beta %*% Beta # indirect effects involving 3 path coefficients
Beta %*% Beta %*% Beta %*% Beta # indirect effects involving 4 path coefficients
## There are none involving 4, so there can't be any higher-order indirect effects

To interpret any nonzero (in)direct path in the matrices above, the variable represented in the row is the outcome, and the variable represented in the column is the predictor.  To view the "total" indirect effect, simply sum all the matrices of indirect effects:

Beta %*% Beta + Beta %*% Beta %*% Beta # + Beta %*% Beta %*% Beta %*% Beta ... if necessary

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: Model comparison with different setting of variables
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan users,

I have difficulties to decide which is a better SEM to be presented in the main part of a paper.

I have two adequate models explaining decomposition process: one includes PCA axis as mediators (PCA-SEM), the other includes individual specific variables (Individual variable SEM). I have these two models because some variables we measured were highly correlated. To avoid collinearity, I took two different ways: 1) construct a PCA then use the axis; 2) grouping the variables based on correlation matrix (grouping is also backed up by PCA) then choose one representative within each group.

The PCA-SEM explained much less variation in decomposition (58%) while the individual variable SEM explained over 70% variation. However, while both SEMs are adequate based on Chi-square, PCA-SEM model is a better fit of the data (RMSEA =0 ( 95 CI 0,0.06), SRMR = 0.047).

Individual variable SEM had RMSEA  of 0.045 (0,0,130) and SRMR of 0.081. AIC values suggest the Individual variable SEM was better.

Is there any way to compare these two non-nested models directly? I understand it is normal to have alternative models, but I would also like to present one in the main text to keep the paper simple.

Besides, is that normal to use PCA axis instead of individual variables in SEM? From my limited reading, I have not seen PCA axis used in SEM.

Thank you in advance for any input!

Hongmei

messages.subject_clean: Confidence intervals for correlations between latent variables
messages.body_plain:
If you report an estimate of a standardized effect, always follow it with a CI for the population standardized effect because the estimate contains sampling error of unknown magnitude and direction.

By the way, this is problematic:

messages.subject_clean: QUARK and MICE
messages.body_plain:
I'm confused.  The script you posted is only about using quark() and imputing the data with mice(). But the problem you described is about fitting a CFA model to data, without specifying whether you are fitting the model to the incomplete data or the imputed data.  I imagine the latter, in which case is there a convergence problem with one or some or all imputed data sets?  Or does the error occur in quark() or mice()? Posting your full script as well as the error would help show exactly where the problem occurs.

>From your description, though, convergence problems with an 80-variable model might not be surprising, depending on your sample size and how well your (probably very restrictive) CFA model actually approximates the data-generating process.  A CFA model with simple structure would try to reproduce 80*(80 - 1)/2 = 3160 observed covariances with only 80 factor loadings and only a few factor correlations (assuming you have multiple factors).  You can probably fit such a model to data simulated from that model, but I doubt real data with such large dimensions would conform to such a simple model, and it might take a large sample to even find a "best" set of estimated parameters.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Help with confidence intervals for standardised regression coefficients
messages.subject_clean: Help with confidence intervals for standardised regression coefficients
messages.body_plain:
> Terrence (or anyone else), what's the reason for using unstandardized coefficients for inferences about a null hypothesis instead of standardized coefficients?

Historically, I think this had something to do with the SEs not being trustworthy when analyzing correlation matrices instead of covariance matrices (at least in certain models without constraining residual variances to be 1 - explained variance).

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.105.2.317

Since null (nil) hypotheses of zero are interpreted the same way for unstandardized and standardized parameters (no effect or relationship), the same hypothesis can be tested using the unstandardized estimate's test statistic or CI.  And the standardized point estimate is used for interpretation, if we don't want reference to an arbitrarily set scale for latent common factors.  Of course, we need to be careful about interpreting standardized effect sizes that way because we use sample estimates of variances to standardize, rather than any known population variance, and variances are also affected by design issues (e.g., how homogeneous is the sampling frame?), so standardized effect sizes are often not comparable across studies anyway. Here's some interesting reading on the subject:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1348/000712608X377117
http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0028086

Of course nowadays, it has been worked out how to calculate unbiased SEs for standardized solutions, but I don't think that means unstandardized solutions should be ignored.  A host of more seasoned SEM veterans on SEMNET might have more to say about this tradition, if you want to try posting this question there:

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

> It would seem strange to me to report the p-value for the unstandardized coefficient together with the estimate and confidence interval for the standardized coefficient.

Well, according to the APA manual, we are expected to report an estimate along with a test statistic, df (if applicable), p value, CI for the estimate, and a standardized measure of effect size.  As Dr. Bonett pointed out, it would be naïve not to report a CI along with the point estimate of a standardized effect size, because those are just as susceptible to sampling variability as unstandardized estimates.  But I am unsure whether normal-theory CIs calculated from SEs for standardized estimates are appropriate, or whether unstandardized confidence limits should be transformed -- maybe the latter is wrong if the sampling variability of estimates used to standardize also need to be considered in the transformation.  Likelihood profile CIs for standardized estimates would be great...  Anyway, I'd love to see literature on this.  Again, SEMNET might be a good place to ask about this, in case someone has already investigated the issue.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: Would variables' position in syntax make differences?
messages.body_plain:
Indeed, you are freely estimating the same parameters in both models:

fit6 <- sem(model6, data=data2, std.lv = TRUE)
fit7 <- sem(model7, data=data2)
all(sort(names(coef(fit6))) ==sort(names(coef(fit7))))

I still don't understand why changing the order of estimated parameters would change convergence, but I think that might just be a coincidence.  You said model6 can be estimated fine, but that came with warnings about Heywood cases, and when you identify the model by fixing factor variances instead of factor loadings, both models converge but cannot estimate SEs.  If you look at your standardized solution for model 6, you will see many correlations beyond 1 and negative variances, as well as extremely poor fit.

summary(fit6, std = TRUE, fit = TRUE)

Inspecting your data gives you some clues as to why your model is so inappropriate.

round(cor(data2[lavNames(fit6)]), digits = 2)

For example, the indicators of attacking correlation more highly with some indicators of skill than with each other, and that will cause factor correlations to skyrocket to try and compensate.  Also, x3 looks like it should be reverse-coded to go in the same direction as the other indicators.  With a mix of positive and negative factor correlations, having a negative factor loading might cause some trouble on its own, even in a model that at least approximates the data-generating process.

> I've tried not to fix this two variances. But the program came to an error.

That is a problem, because your model should be identified just with the fixed factor loadings.  If a model fits very poorly, the optimizer may never find a "best" solution because no good one exists.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> Are these Aux variables reliable to use for imputation?

Not sure.  I have only read one methodological study on this method, using only 8 variables.  It was a good proof of concept, but I'm not sure how well it "scales up" to larger dimensions like you are using -- which is of course the whole benefit of using this method to reduce the dimensionality of auxiliaries.

Note that you could also just save the columns of principal components that are output in the single imputation.  Save them to your original data set, then use them as auxiliaries in a FIML analysis.  FIML is more efficient than multiple imputation anyway, so it is usually preferable.  Unless you can't use FIML (e.g., with categorical outcomes).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Hello everybody,
I am having some troubles with fitting a bi-factor model on my WISC-IV data. In fact, my model sldModBif did not converge, and I was wondering weather my syntax is wrong.

Moreover, after looking at the theta matrix, I decided to fix one parameter to 0 (model wiscBifactor2). I am a little bit worried because I want to estimate omega and omega hierarchical and I just want to be sure that this model is ok.

Furthermore, is there any builtin function to calculate the omega, the hierarchical omega and the omega s (i.e., consistency reliability associated with subscale scores) (Reise et al., 2012)?

#sld
sldCor<-lower2full(c(
1,
+ .338, 1,
+ .111, .173, 1,
+ .255, .340, .117, 1,
+ .059, -.023, .063, .073, 1,
+ .257, .578, .184, .250, .036, 1,
+ .184, .209, .358, .198, .118, .230, 1,
+ .415, .299, .180, .353, .124, .255, .262, 1,
+ .187, .473, .173, .224, .030, .539, .222, .173, 1,
+ .189, .100, .067, .152, .453, .052, .159, .229, .078, 1))

sldSd<-c(2.853, 3.042, 2.521, 3.018, 2.855, 3.046, 2.620, 3.070, 3.410, 2.845)
colnames(sldCor)<-rownames(sldCor)<-c("BD","SI","DS","PCm","CD","VC","LN","MR","CO","SS")
sldCov<-cor2cov(sldCor,sldSd)

wiscBifactor <- '
# domain specific factors
PRI =~ BD + PCm + MR
VCI =~ SI + VC + CO
WMI =~ a*DS + a*LN
PSI =~ b*CD + b*SS
# general factor
g =~ BD + PCm + MR + SI + VC + CO + DS + LN + CD + SS
'
wiscBifactor2 <- '
# first-order factors
VCI =~ SI + VC + CO
PRI =~ PCm + MR + BD
WMI =~ b*DS + b*LN
PSI =~ c*CD + c*SS
# second-order factor
g =~ BD + PCm + MR + SI + VC + CO + DS + LN + CD + SS
MR ~~ 0*MR
'

sldModBif<- sem(model=wiscBifactor,sample.cov=sldCov,sample.nobs=910,std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,orthogonal=TRUE)
inspect(sldModBif,"theta")
sldModBif2<- sem(model=wiscBifactor2,sample.cov=sldCov,sample.nobs=910,std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,orthogonal=TRUE)

Thank you very much for any help you can provide,
Best,
David

messages.body_plain:
Factor loadings are estimated based on the covariances between observed variables. If you allow residual covariances between all of those same observed variables, then neither the loadings nor the residual covariances can be uniquely estimated. If you want to estimate the loadings, then delete the lines that enable residual covariances.

messages.body_plain:
> 1) is it advisable to fix one theta to zero to fit the model, or this is likely to have important consequences on the model estimation?

I'm not sure I understand.  Do you have a single-indicator construct that requires its indicator's residual variance to be fixed?  If you aren't estimating reliability for a single-indicator construct, I would just leave it out of the model for reliability estimation of the relevant constructs.

> 2) thanks for the omega hierarchical. as for the omega s (i.e., consistency reliability associated with subscale scores; see below), as far as I can see it is not calculated with the reliability function.  is there any other function, or do I have to calculate it by hand?

Using the example on the ?reliability help page, all 3 omegas are returned for each individual construct, as well as a "total" reliability for a single composite calculated from all items in the model.  Are you talking about something else?  Posting your path diagram might help illustrate what you want that you aren't getting.  If you want a reliability estimate for a composite of items that partials out the one of the factors, then yes, you will have to calculate that by hand.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> fit6 <- sem(COS.pan3, data = cos, estimator = "ML", missing = "fiml")
> fitsemaux <- sem.auxiliary(fit6, data = cos, aux = auxvars, estimator="ML", missing="FIML")

Hi Giovanni, I know you are using the latest development version of semTools since we've been in contact about runMI() :-)  If you take a look at the ?auxiliary help page, you will see that auxiliary() only accepts a character vector or parameter table, not a previously fitted lavaan object as in previous versions of semTools (that introduces too many potential problems).  So this should work fine:

fitsemaux <- sem.auxiliary(COS.pan3, data = cos, aux = auxvars)

The estimator and missing arguments are unnecessary because they are implied by the use of auxiliary().

FYI, since you are fitting invariance models, be aware that if you constrain measurement parameters using the group.equal argument, then "intercepts" will also constrain the intercepts (means) of auxiliaries and "residuals" will also constrain the variances of auxiliaries, because those keywords operate on any observed (non-latent, non-exogenous) variables in the model.  So the invariance models will be too restrictive and result in Type I errors.

Until I figure out a way to get around the group.equal issue, the way to avoid this problem is to apply equality constraints in the syntax instead, by giving parameters the same label.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> I read through the post several times and realized my case was different from theirs. As I have the same number of variables in both models, I will simply use BIC to decide which stays in the main text.

The issue is not whether the number of variables is the same.  The issue is whether the variables are the same.  These two models have the same number of variables, but not the same variables:

> Y ~ X + A
> A ~ X
>
> vs.
>
> Y ~ X + B
> B ~ X

BIC can't be used to compare those two models because the mediator is a different variable, even though the structure of the model is identical.

Hello!

Google seemed silent about it, so now I have a question for the lavaan package maintainers and associated folks, either Yves, Sunthud, or Terry (you are doing an incredible job!):

When using lavaan-0.5-23.1097 and running a cross-sectional MI test (MGCFA with 9 groups and WLSMV estimation):

    models.cat <http://models.cat>    <- list( fit.configural = fit.cat.configural,  fit.loadings = fit.cat.metric )
    fit.cat.pame  <- partialInvarianceCat(models.cat <http://models.cat>, type = "metric", return.fit = TRUE, method = "satorra.2000")

I don't have a problem at, and the output will show up as expected.

However, when running:

    models.cat <http://models.cat>   <- list( fit.loadings = fit.cat.metric, fit.thresholds = fit.cat.scalar )
    fit <- partialInvarianceCat(models.cat <http://models.cat>, type = "scalar", return.fit = TRUE, method = "satorra.2000")

I quickly get:

    Error in if (!any(parTable$lhs == newline$lhs & parTable$op == newline$op &  :
    missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

I am at a loss here. I does not matter whether the models themselves stem from manually fitted model (via cfa-function) or obtaining them automatically (via measurementInvarianceCat function).

The only hint to the specific code I could find stems from a github page that refers to longitudinal invariance:
https://github.com/simsem/semTools/blob/master/semTools/R/longInvariance.R (line 399)

This part pertains to the constrainParTable function. It appears that this function is also called several times from the partialInvarianceCat-Function (e.g., line 160 etc.).

             if (dup[i]) {
                    pt0 <- constrainParTable(pt0, facinfix[i],
                      "=~", fix[i], 1:ngroups)
                    pt1 <- constrainParTable(pt1, facinfix[i],
                      "=~", fix[i], 1:ngroups)

Still, I cannot understand what is going on, since the models converged normally (quite a bit of iterations, but nonetheless ...):

               Length Class  Mode
fit.configural 1      lavaan S4
fit.loadings   1      lavaan S4
fit.thresholds 1      lavaan S4
fit.means      1      lavaan S4

Whether the models are defined in a simple manner for the MICat-Function or rather complex (following the Millsap & Yun-Tein approach manually) also doesn't make a difference. Neither does strict=TRUE vs FALSE.

Has anybody encountered this before (and knows a potential solution) and can guide me in the right direction? Or is this a bug?

Many thanks in advance!
Matthias Bluemke

messages.body_plain:
> Yves, Sunthud, or Terry (you are doing an incredible job!):

Thanks!

> When using lavaan-0.5-23.1097

I doubt the problem is a version issue, but the latest development version of lavaan is in the 0.6 family, and semTools has been updated to cooperate with internal lavaan changes.

install.packages("lavaan", repos = "http://www.da.ugent.be", type = "source")
devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

> However, when running:
>     models.cat <http://models.cat>   <- list( fit.loadings = fit.cat.metric, fit.thresholds = fit.cat.scalar )
>     fit <- partialInvarianceCat(models.cat <http://models.cat>, type = "scalar", return.fit = TRUE, method = "satorra.2000")

Since the problem only occurs when comparing scalar and metric models, I have to wonder whether it is an identification issue.  Do you have binary indicators?

> I does not matter whether the models themselves stem from manually fitted model (via cfa-function) or obtaining them automatically (via measurementInvarianceCat function).

It would only matter if you specify the models differently than the measurementInvarianceCat function does.

> Still, I cannot understand what is going on, since the models converged normally

But the partialInvariance function fits more multiple models (i.e., each item freed from the scalar one at a time, and each item fixed from the metric one at a time).  If the hidden constrainParTable function is the culprit, you can try the debug function to see what is happening leading up to the failure.

debug(semTools:::constrainParTable)

When you are done using it, make sure to turn it off

undebug(semTools:::constrainParTable)

> Whether the models are defined in a simple manner for the MICat-Function or rather complex (following the Millsap & Yun-Tein approach manually) also doesn't make a difference.

The measurementInvarianceCat function does implement the Millsap & Yun-Tein approach.  Have you tried manually fitting a model using constraints more typically applied to continuous indicators, as seen here?

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.882658

The sequence of models are statistically equivalent, but in simulations I've noticed Millsap & Yun-Tein's identification suggestions sometimes lead to convergence problems where the model as fit in Sass et al. (linked above) converge fine.  Maybe you just have a data set that doesn't cooperate with their identification suggestions, which are being called into question anyway since a recent Psychometrika article went into much greater depth on this topic

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11336-016-9506-0

> Neither does strict=TRUE vs FALSE.

Your error does not occur with the strict model anyway, or in the measurementInvarianceCat function at all, just the partial function, right?

> Has anybody encountered this before (and knows a potential solution) and can guide me in the right direction? Or is this a bug?

The example with ordinal data on the help page works fine.  The binary-data example does not work because this:

modelsCat <- list(configural = outConfigural2, metric = outWeak2)

should be changed to this:

modelsCat <- list(fit.configural = outConfigural2, fit.loadings = outWeak2)

So if you can't find the problem with debug(), I would probably need access to your data to find the problem.  A solution, however, would be to just not rely on the partial function and instead test the constraints manually, using your preferred among the 3 approaches offered by partialInvariance().  I always thought this function was exploratory overkill anyway, and have considered changing it to only return tests from one method at a time (to save computing time, if nothing else).  But I probably won't get around to changing it before 2018.  Anyway, a quick-and-dirty way to use the "group.equal" argument to impose equality constraints on measurement parameters, and loop over the indicators to free one item at a time with the "group.partial" argument. Something like this should work:

for (i in lavNames(fit.scalar, type = "ov.ind")) {
  print(anova(fit.scalar, update(fit.scalar, group.partial = paste0(i, "~1"))))
}

messages.body_plain:
hi,

I have some problems establishing measurement invariance model to my data and I hope I can find some help here. I try to fit a 1 factor 4 indicator model along Millsaps advice and the code provided by Sunthud (http://www.sunthud.com/catInvariance.html).

in order to narrow down the reason for convergence problems (i get these or very small SEs resulting in extremely large z-values) i stepwise added the constraints proposed by Millsap and the model seems to crash only when i constrain the indicator variances to 1 in the reference group and release them in group 2. Yves meant that the theta parameterization can lead to numerical issues and i suspect that the extremely skewed data is the culprit for my issues. Is there something i can do about it?

under MLR the results from measurement invariance analysis are quite good, also when i apply the (not anymore recommended?) way of constraining loadings and thresholds via group.equal. However, reviewers asked me how i handled the problem that loadings and thresholds can't be constrained independently from each other (i have not so far) and suggested that MLR is not appropriate for ordinal data. The paper referenced today in the other thread about partialinvariancecat() suggest that it's not so simple.

Finally, it would be great if someone could explain like i am 5 why i can estimate mgcfa models without imposing millsaps constraints on thresholds which are thought to identify the model - shouldn't a non-identified model be difficult to estimate?

Find attached some of my data (my final model has some more groups, factors and indicators, but the problems already appear in such a small part of the model) and code:

library(lavaan)
dat = read.table("test.txt", header = TRUE)

model0 = "Fac1 =~ P3_1 + P3_2 + P3_3 + P3_4"
model1 =
  "Fac1 =~ P3_1 + P3_2 + P3_3 + P3_4
P3_1 |  c(t1P3_1, t1P3_1) *t1 + c(t2P3_1, t2P3_1)*t2 + t3 + t4
P3_2 |  c(t1P3_2, t1P3_2) *t1 + t2 + t3 + t4

"
model2 =
  "Fac1 =~ P3_1 + P3_2 + P3_3 + P3_4
P3_1 |  c(t1P3_1, t1P3_1) *t1 + c(t2P3_1, t2P3_1)*t2 + t3 + t4
P3_2 |  c(t1P3_2, t1P3_2) *t1 + t2 + t3 + t4
P3_3 |  c(t1P3_3, t1P3_3) *t1 + t2 + t3 + t4
P3_4 |  c(t1P3_4, t1P3_4) *t1 + t2 + t3 + t4
Fac1 ~ c(0,NA)*1
"

model3 =
  "Fac1 =~ P3_1 + P3_2 + P3_3 + P3_4
P3_1 |  c(t1P3_1, t1P3_1) *t1 + c(t2P3_1, t2P3_1)*t2 + t3 + t4
P3_2 |  c(t1P3_2, t1P3_2) *t1 + t2 + t3 + t4
P3_3 |  c(t1P3_3, t1P3_3) *t1 + t2 + t3 + t4
P3_4 |  c(t1P3_4, t1P3_4) *t1 + t2 + t3 + t4
Fac1 ~ c(0,NA)*1
Fac1 ~~ c(NA,NA)*Fac1
"
model4 =
  "Fac1 =~ P3_1 + P3_2 + P3_3 + P3_4
P3_1 |  c(t1P3_1, t1P3_1) *t1 + c(t2P3_1, t2P3_1)*t2 + t3 + t4
P3_2 |  c(t1P3_2, t1P3_2) *t1 + t2 + t3 + t4
P3_3 |  c(t1P3_3, t1P3_3) *t1 + t2 + t3 + t4
P3_4 |  c(t1P3_4, t1P3_4) *t1 + t2 + t3 + t4
Fac1 ~ c(0,NA)*1
Fac1 ~~ c(NA,NA)*Fac1
P3_1 ~~ c(1, NA)*P3_1
P3_2 ~~ c(1, NA)*P3_2
P3_3 ~~ c(1, NA)*P3_3
P3_4 ~~ c(1, NA)*P3_4
"

models = list(model0, model1, model2, model3,model4)
x = lapply(models, function(y) cfa(y, data = dat, group = "COUNTRY", ordered = c("P3_1", "P3_2", "P3_3", "P3_4"), parameterization = "theta"))
summary(x[[4]])
summary(x[[5]])

Thanks for looking into this, best, felix

messages.body_plain:
> In case it's not entirely clear: i already fail to fit the configural invariant model.

A colleague and I also found convergence issues with Millsap & Yun-Tein's identification method when we fit it to simulated data, where a statistically equivalent model converged fine (i.e., the "usual" configural invariance model, as fit by Sass et al. <http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10705511.2014.882658>, with fixed intercepts and factor means/variances, and free loadings and thresholds -- either the delta or theta parameterizations converged normally even when Millsap & Yun-Tein's model did not).  A recent Psychometrika article has finally extended that research and gone into much greater depth, calling into question Millsap & Yun-Tein's advice.

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11336-016-9506-0

Wu and Estabrook (2016) showed that equivalence of particular parameters can never be tested alone because imposing constraints on those parameters typically allows other parameters to be freed, which were previously fixed for identification purposes only.  They therefore recommend (a) starting with a test of thresholds, for reasons you can read at the above link, and (b) potentially using a different pair of models for each type of parameters to be tested for equivalence.  Given you have 4 thresholds, I will tell you the practical advice that I took away from reading the article, based on their Figure 1 (p., 1034).  Since Millsap & Yun-Tein's model did not converge for on your data, you can fit a baseline model that is the default in the cfa(..., std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE) function (fix factor variances and means, use either delta or theta parameterization, fix intercepts, free loadings and thresholds).  Then test equivalence of thresholds using a model with the following specification:
fix factor variances and means to 1 and 0, respectively, in all groups
free loadings in all groups
free intercepts in all but one group (fix to zero in reference group)
using delta or theta parameterization, the residual variances in the reference group will be fixed such that the total or residual variance (respectively) will be fixed to 1.  But in all other groups, you can free the latent-response scales or residual variances, respectively.  I would recommend using theta (as Millsap & Yun-Tein's suggested) so you can work with residual variances instead of latent-response scales.
After this, testing additional levels of invariance is straight-forward (because your indicators have > 3 categories).  To the model with equal thresholds, simply add the additional constraint that loadings are equivalent and free factor variances in all but the reference group, then test the nested model.  To that model, you can add the additional constraint that intercepts are equivalent and free factor means in all but the reference group, then test the nested model.  If you are interested in testing strict invariance, to either the metric/weak or scalar/strong model, you can add the additional constraint that residual variances are equal across groups, then test nested models.

If you have only 2 or 3 categories, then not every type of parameter could be tested for equivalence without assuming other measurement parameters are also invariant.

Hope this helps,

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> Anyway, i can't really wrap my head around the reason why there are different approaches to configural invariance.

It is still an open area of research, but moving relatively slowly in the factor analysis literature.  Much more work on latent trait models with categorical indicators has been (and is being) done in the IRT literature.  The advantages of SEM are great, but having categorical indicators means we not only have latent common factors, but additional latent response variables (one per binary/ordinal indicator).  The latent response variables have the same location/scale-identification issues that common factors have, but it is even more restrictive because there are not multiple indicators of the latent responses -- it is just an assumed normal variable underlying the discretized observed variable.  Anyway, I agree, it is frustratingly complicated.  The Wu & Estabrook (2016) article is a breath of fresh air, but it really just clarified the problem, and the field still needs to work out what the "best practices" should be.  "Watch this space" :-)

> Yves wrote me that Millsap and Yun-Teins approach might be actually less constrained than cfa(..., group = "g").

The models are statistically equivalent, but M & Y-T wanted to identify the model without assuming equality of common-factor means/variances or residual variances (although they seemed fine with assuming intercepts were equivalent).

> I figured that the nice property of Millsap and Yun-Teins approach might be that the latent factor means can be actually compared with a minimal set of constraints, whereas under the other approaches those have to be fixed to 0,1? Is that true?

No, the latent distributions (means & (co)variances) can still only be compared meaningfully across groups if the measurement parameters are constrained to equality (just like with continuous indicators).  So M & Y-T's method seems like an unnecessary exercise in defining a "less restrictive" statistically equivalent model to the standard default cfa(..., group = "g").

> I got the request from reviewers to actually compare the impact of imposing constraints over groups on factor scores - is that a sensible thing to do?  Wouldn't be the comparison unfair in models where both groups have the 0,1 constraint on the latent variable?

Yes, but when you constrain measurement parameters across groups, then you only need to fix the common-factor means/variances to 0/1 in a single group, freely estimating them in the remaining groups.

Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> how do I extract predicted probabilities from a regression of an observed endogenous categorical variable?

You can't.  lavaan's predict() method returns estimates of factor scores, and the fitted() method returns model-implied (predicted) summary statistics.  So these are not like the predict/fitted methods for a lm or glm object.  But you can manually calculate predicted probabilities conditional on any values of "lv" that you want, but plugging those values into the equation for probits (also plugging in the model estimates), then using pnorm() to transform the probits into cumulative probabilities.

> I know that it is possible for lavaan to mimic the output of EQS but I dont think that is the input needed to generate the plots.

Unfortunately correct, the mimic option is basically just about using N-1 (Wishart likelihood) instead of N (normal likelihood) when calculating SEs and chi-squared.  The semdaig package is designed literally only to run EQS from R, grab output from an EQS file, and manipulate it to produce semdaig output.  You could write the authors of the package about the possibility of adapting the package to work with lavaan models (assuming lavaan provides what is necessary).  I know they work with lavaan in other contexts, so it's possible only EQS provides what is necessary for it to work (which is something they could request Yves to make available from lavInspect()).  But it's possible they already have unpublished code they are willing to share with you that will work with lavaan models, and they could contact me about adding it to semTools.

Sharada--
     You will find this concern expressed in places like the Mplus manual. Yes, you can eliminate the problem by dividing a variable with a large variance by some constant, like a power of 10--or multiplying a variable with a small variance by a power of 10. Using a constant in this way will have no statistical "side effects."
     The large negative loading for one indicator of TRAIT is a classical symptom of a model not converging. Rescaling *may* eliminate the problem. You might also consider setting a starting value for this loading: 1 if you expect a positive loading or -1 if you expect a negative loading.

messages.body_plain:
The M.I. and EPC statistic assume that no other parameter estimates will change value when the one constraint is removed. If you fixed all current parameter estimates at their current values but removed the one constraint, M.I. and EPC would hit the mark, pretty much exactly. M.I. is a derivative of the one constraint only, not a multivariate derivative.

messages.subject_clean: A question of 'estmodel.sem' in simsem
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I found that people have asked questions about simsem here and thus let me post my questions here. Specifically, I am trying to use the estmodel.sem command. However, R gave the following error message:

loading2 <- matrix(0, 18, 3)
loading2[1:6, 1] <- NA
loading2[7:12, 2] <- NA
loading2[13:18, 3] <- NA

factor.cor2 <- diag(3)
factor.cor2[1, 2] <- factor.cor2[2, 1] <- NA

path2 <- matrix(0, 2, 3)
path2[1:2, 3] <- NA

RTE2 <- diag(18)

analyze.model2 <- estmodel.sem(LY=loading2, RPS=factor.cor2,
                               BE=path2, RTE=RTE2
                               )

ERROR MESSAGE:
Error in bind(free = free, popParam = popParam, misspec = misspec, symmetric = symmetric) :
  A vector cannot be symmetric

I am unsure why it occurs. I figured out that it has something about RPS, because it seems to work if I exclude RPS in the estmodel.sem command. In RPS, I am trying to model the latent covariance/correlation between the disturbances of two endogeneous factors.

Thanks for your help!

Chester

messages.subject: Re: Coefficients that reverse sign when entering SEM
messages.subject_clean: Coefficients that reverse sign when entering SEM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hila,

Looks like a suppression situation.  Which variable you consider a "suppressor" might be as arbitrary as which variable in an interaction you consider the "moderator".  Here is some reading on the subject:

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1026595011371

Since this question has nothing to do with lavaan, you would probably have more luck getting advice from the much larger forum of SEM experts on SEMNET:

www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> I am unsure why it occurs. I figured out that it has something about RPS, because it seems to work if I exclude RPS in the estmodel.sem command.

Indeed, you stumbled on a bug.  Thanks for catching it.  I fixed it, and your example now works in the development version of simsem.  If you have the devtools package installed, you can use this syntax to install the development version:

devtools::install_github("simsem/simsem/simsem")

FYI, there is a problem in your syntax.  Beta and Psi need to be the same dimension, so you use:

path2 <- matrix(0, 3, 3)

path2[1:2, 3] <- NA
